title: Classification / Odd One Out — In-Depth Guide

questions.question: What is the first step in the guide's classification-solving flow (Find GROUP -> Find PROPERTY -> Find EXCEPTION -> ANSWER)?
options: Identify the group the majority of items belong to
Immediately eliminate the longest word
Guess the odd one out by instinct
Count the letters in every option first
questions.rationale: The guide's solving flow starts by finding the shared group among the majority of items, then the specific property that defines it, before checking which single item breaks that property.

questions.question: When a classification group has no obvious shared meaning, what should you check instead?
options: Give up and pick the first option
Whether the words rhyme
Structural properties, such as letter count or numeric properties like perfect squares/primes
The alphabetical order of the options
questions.rationale: Many classification questions hide a structural or numeric pattern rather than a meaning-based one — checking letter counts, perfect squares, primes, and similar properties often reveals the real shared category.

questions.question: In the set 121, 144, 169, 200, 225, why is 200 the odd one out?
options: It is the only even number
It is the only number that is not a perfect square
It is the only three-digit number
It is the largest number in the set
questions.rationale: 121, 144, 169, and 225 are perfect squares (11^2, 12^2, 13^2, 15^2); 200 is not a perfect square, breaking the shared structural property.

questions.question: If your first guess at the shared category leaves more than one item looking 'odd,' what should you do?
options: Pick either odd item at random
Switch to checking only alphabetical order
Conclude the question has no valid answer
Refine or narrow the category definition until exactly one item fails it
questions.rationale: A correct classification category should leave exactly one item as the exception — if more than one item seems to fail your guessed category, the category itself needs to be made more specific.

questions.question: What does 'Classification by Last-Digit Parity' test?
options: Whether a group of numbers' last digits are all consistently odd (or all even), with one breaking that pattern
Whether numbers share the same first digit
Whether numbers are all prime
Whether numbers are all perfect squares
questions.rationale: This tests whether the last digits of a group of numbers are consistently odd or consistently even, identifying the number whose last digit breaks that parity pattern.

questions.question: What does 'Classification by First Digit' test, in contrast to last digit?
options: The same property as last digit
A digit-count property
Whether a group of numbers all share the same first (leading) digit, with one number starting differently
A prime-factorization property
questions.rationale: This tests whether numbers all share the same leading digit, identifying the number that starts with a different digit.

questions.question: What does 'Classification by Digit Order' test?
options: A first-digit property only
Whether a group of numbers' digits follow a consistent internal order pattern (e.g., increasing), with one number breaking it
A last-digit property only
A prime-factorization property
questions.rationale: This tests whether each number's own digits follow a consistent internal ordering pattern, such as increasing left to right, identifying the exception.

questions.question: What does 'Classification by Digit Difference' test?
options: A digit-sum property
A prime-position property
A digit-product property
Whether a group of numbers share a consistent difference between specific digits (e.g., first minus last), with one number breaking it
questions.rationale: This tests whether numbers share a consistent numeric gap between specific digit positions, identifying the number whose digit difference doesn't match.

questions.question: What does 'Classification by Number of Letters' (applied to number NAMES) test?
options: Whether the WRITTEN-OUT names of a group of numbers (like 'seven') share a common letter count, with one breaking that pattern
The numeric value directly
A digit-sum property
A prime-factorization property
questions.rationale: This tests the letter count of numbers' spelled-out names (like 'seven' having 5 letters), identifying the number whose written name has a different letter count.

questions.question: What does 'Classification by Number-Name Letters' build on from the 'Number Names' concept?
options: Only the numeric digit value
Only whether the number is even or odd
The specific letters used in a number's spelled-out name, applying letter-based classification techniques to those written names
A property unrelated to number names
questions.rationale: This applies letter-based classification techniques (like shared letters or patterns) to numbers' spelled-out names, rather than to their numeric digit values directly.

questions.question: What does the 'Advanced Classification Framework' near the end of the lesson consolidate?
options: Only the most basic single-property checks
The full range of techniques covered (property types, elimination, feature vectors, invariants) into one comprehensive solving framework
A framework unrelated to classification
Only number-based techniques
questions.rationale: This consolidates the full range of techniques covered throughout the lesson — property types, elimination, feature vectors, invariants — into one comprehensive framework.

questions.question: What does 'Classification Priority Order' establish?
options: A random order to check properties in
An order unrelated to solving efficiency
That only one property type should ever be checked
A recommended sequence for checking candidate properties, generally starting with the simplest/most common types first
questions.rationale: This establishes a recommended order for checking candidate properties, generally starting with the simplest and most commonly-tested types before moving to more complex ones.

questions.question: Why does 'the simplest rule usually win' in classification, as this lesson explains?
options: Because complex rules are always wrong
Because a genuinely intended classification question is almost always built around a clear, straightforward shared property rather than an obscure one
Because simple rules are easier to guess randomly
Because complexity has no bearing on correctness
questions.rationale: Well-constructed classification questions are almost always built around a clear, straightforward shared property, making the simplest consistent rule the most likely correct one.

questions.question: When is a 'complex rule' actually necessary, according to this lesson?
options: Never — complex rules are always wrong
When no simple property is consistently supported by all-but-one items, requiring a more nuanced or combined property to explain the pattern
Complex rules are always preferred over simple ones
Only for letter-based classification
questions.rationale: A complex rule becomes necessary only when no simple property can be found that's genuinely and consistently supported by all-but-one of the items.
